Principles and Political Power: The Debate Over Roy Moore’s Senate Campaign

In the weeks before Alabama’s December 2017 special election, allegations against Republican Senate candidate Roy Moore became a central issue in the campaign. Several women said Moore had pursued them when they were teenagers, and one woman alleged that he sexually assaulted her when she was 16. Moore denied the allegations and said he had not engaged in sexual misconduct.

Alabama voters therefore faced a choice shaped not only by party politics but also by questions about credibility, character and the standards candidates should meet. Moore’s Democratic opponent, Doug Jones, argued that the allegations disqualified Moore from serving in the Senate. Moore and many of his Republican supporters rejected the accusations and described them as politically motivated.

The controversy created a difficult situation for Republican leaders. Some national Republicans withdrew their support or called on Moore to leave the race, while others continued to back him because they believed a Republican victory was important to the party’s control of the Senate. President Donald Trump ultimately endorsed Moore and urged Alabama voters to support him.

The dispute also revived broader arguments about the Republican Party’s emphasis on family values and personal responsibility. Critics said that supporting Moore despite the allegations would undermine the party’s stated positions on sexual misconduct and accountability. Supporters responded that the allegations had not been established in court and that voters should decide the matter.

The allegations against Moore also drew attention to the different standards Republicans had applied to prominent Democrats, including former President Bill Clinton. At the same time, critics noted that Trump had won the 2016 presidential election despite multiple women publicly accusing him of sexual misconduct. Trump denied the accusations, and he has not been criminally charged in connection with them.

The debate reflected a broader struggle within the Republican Party over whether electoral victories should take precedence over questions of conduct. Some Republicans viewed the Alabama contest primarily as a referendum on party control of the Senate and the policies of the Trump administration. Others argued that a candidate’s character and the credibility of accusations against him should be considered independently of political consequences.

The election also took place amid a national reckoning over sexual harassment and assault. In 2017, allegations against powerful figures in entertainment, media, politics and business led to public discussions about workplace misconduct, the treatment of accusers and the responsibilities of institutions that protect influential people.

Supporters of Moore said that the allegations should be evaluated carefully and that unproven claims should not automatically determine an election. Critics said the accounts were serious enough to require political accountability even without a criminal conviction. The disagreement illustrated the difficulty of balancing due process with the responsibility of political parties to decide whom they will support.

Alabama’s electorate was also being viewed through the lens of the state’s political history. The contest was held in a state that had voted reliably Republican in recent presidential elections, but Democrats believed Jones had a chance because of the controversy surrounding Moore and the state’s history of electing Democratic officials. Jones was a former federal prosecutor who had led the successful prosecution of two men responsible for the 1963 bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham.

The campaign attracted national attention because the result could affect the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans held a narrow majority, and a Moore victory would have preserved one of the party’s seats. A Jones victory would have reduced the Republican majority and offered Democrats an opportunity to challenge the party in a traditionally conservative state.

The controversy also prompted discussion about the future of the Republican Party. The United States was becoming more racially and culturally diverse, and younger voters and women were increasingly influential in national elections. Political analysts and party officials had differing views about how Republicans should respond to those changes, including whether the party should focus primarily on conservative policy positions or make broader efforts to appeal to voters who felt alienated by its rhetoric and candidates.

Those questions extended beyond the Moore campaign. Political parties routinely face conflicts between ideological goals, electoral strategy and standards of conduct. Decisions made during high-profile campaigns can influence public perceptions of a party for years, particularly when leaders appear to apply different rules to allies and opponents.

The debate over Moore also underscored the limits of comparisons with earlier Republican figures, including Abraham Lincoln. Lincoln’s presidency is associated with the preservation of the Union and the abolition of slavery, but invoking his legacy does not resolve contemporary disputes over candidates or party policy. Historical accomplishments cannot substitute for evaluating present-day allegations and political decisions on their own terms.

Ultimately, Alabama voters were asked to decide whether Moore should represent them in the Senate. They could treat the allegations as disqualifying, accept Moore’s denials, or weigh the accusations alongside their views on party control and policy. The decision belonged to voters, while the responsibility for presenting accurate information rested with the candidates, political organizations and news media covering the race.

On December 12, 2017, Jones defeated Moore in the special election. The result was widely attributed to a combination of factors, including the allegations against Moore, Democratic turnout and the Republican candidate’s difficulty consolidating support. Moore continued to deny wrongdoing after the election.

The Alabama campaign did not settle the larger questions raised during it. Political parties continued to face scrutiny over how they respond to allegations against candidates and officeholders, particularly when those individuals are important to the party’s electoral goals. The episode demonstrated that political power and institutional credibility can come into direct conflict, and that voters may make decisions based on both policy preferences and judgments about character.

The agreement also describes discussions about arranging a meeting between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Second, the timing of Papadopoulos’s outreach has drawn attention. Donald Trump’s attorney Jay Sekulow defended the president during a Tuesday morning interview with ABC host George Stephanopoulos, arguing that the term “collusion” does not itself describe a specific criminal offense.

The Numbers Are In: 2018 Obamacare Premiums Reflected Both Market Pressures and Trump Administration Policy

Donald Trump said health insurance premiums were rising and blamed Democrats for the Affordable Care Act. But analyses of the 2018 individual market found that several factors were affecting premiums, including medical costs, insurer participation, uncertainty over federal policy and the administration’s decision to stop reimbursing insurers for cost-sharing reductions.

Premiums were expected to increase in many parts of the country even without the policy changes. Insurers had cited rising claims costs and uncertainty surrounding the ACA’s future when submitting their 2018 rates. However, many insurers also said the end of cost-sharing-reduction payments would require them to raise premiums, particularly for plans sold on the individual market.

An analysis published by Charles Gaba, an independent health-care data analyst, estimated that nationwide unsubsidized premiums would have risen by about 12 percent without the additional policy uncertainty. His estimate rose to roughly 16 percent under what he described as partial disruption and nearly 30 percent under a scenario in which the administration took several actions affecting the law.

Those figures were estimates based on Gaba’s methodology, rather than official government calculations. The impact varied substantially by state.

WASHINGTON: Gaba estimated that unsubsidized rates would have increased by about 26 percent without the additional uncertainty and by roughly 36 percent after accounting for the administration’s policy decisions.

VIRGINIA: His estimates were approximately 43 percent without the added disruption and 58 percent with it.

TENNESSEE: Gaba estimated an increase of about 14 percent without the added uncertainty and nearly 29 percent with it.

In North Carolina, insurers largely responded to the loss of cost-sharing-reduction payments by adding the resulting costs to premiums for silver plans. That design choice contributed to particularly large increases for some unsubsidized consumers, although the exact effect depended on the plan and rating area.

Other estimates showed similar effects. Gaba’s analysis placed New Mexico’s projected increase at roughly 15 percent without the additional policy changes and about 30 percent with them. His estimates for Arkansas were approximately 9 percent and 18 percent, respectively. For California, he estimated increases of about 12 percent without the added uncertainty and 17 percent with it. Colorado’s figures were roughly 28 percent and 34 percent.

The analysis distinguished between unsubsidized consumers and people receiving premium tax credits. Subsidized consumers were generally protected from the full effect of premium increases because the size of their tax credits also rose with benchmark premiums. Unsubsidized consumers, including some middle-income people who did not qualify for assistance, faced the largest direct impact.

The Kaiser Family Foundation also concluded that insurers’ decisions to raise premiums were influenced by the administration’s announcement that it would end cost-sharing-reduction payments. In many states, insurers added the cost to silver plans, while some states spread it across plans or used other approaches. The result was a wide range of premium changes around the country.

The market had also been affected by broader uncertainty over whether the ACA would remain in place, as well as by the administration’s decision to reduce funding for enrollment outreach and advertising. Those actions did not independently determine every rate increase, and premiums differed according to local competition, insurer participation and the health of each state’s market.

Republicans and the administration argued that the increases demonstrated weaknesses in the ACA. Democrats and consumer advocates responded that the federal government’s policy decisions had contributed to the higher rates and market uncertainty.

The 2018 figures therefore did not establish that one party alone was responsible for every premium increase. They showed that insurers were responding to both underlying market conditions and significant changes in federal policy. For consumers, the effect depended largely on whether they received financial assistance and on how their state and insurers handled the loss of the cost-sharing payments.

The agreement stated that government entities would not have the right to “audit or review the cost and profit elements” of the contract, prompting questions about oversight of the deal, which was valued at up to roughly $300 million.

The contract also set daily allowances for lodging and meals and established hourly rates for workers. Supervisors were to be paid $462 per hour, while linemen were to receive $319 per hour, according to the agreement. The terms attracted criticism because of the company’s relatively small size and limited prior experience with government contracts.

The contract further stated that the Puerto Rican government would waive claims against Whitefish related to delays in completing the work. Critics said the provision reduced the government’s leverage if power restoration took longer than expected.

San Juan Mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz called for the agreement to be voided. After Cruz criticized the arrangement, Whitefish said on Twitter that it had 44 linemen working in the city and that additional workers had arrived, asking whether the mayor wanted them to continue.

Cruz responded that the company’s message was inappropriate and said the contract should be canceled in favor of a process that was “clear, transparent, legal, moral and ethical,” according to comments reported by Yahoo News.

The agreement also raised concerns in Congress. Reps. Rob Bishop and Bruce Westerman, the Republican chairman and chairman of a subcommittee of the House Natural Resources Committee, wrote that the contract’s size and terms, along with the circumstances in which it was formed, raised questions about PREPA’s contracting procedures.

Whitefish said it welcomed congressional inquiries and defended its ability and commitment to help restore electricity and normalcy to Puerto Rico. Before the agreement, the company’s largest government contract had reportedly been a $1.3 million project to upgrade power lines in Arizona.

The controversy intensified as federal and Puerto Rican officials examined the contract and the island’s broader response to the hurricane. PREPA ultimately canceled the agreement on October 29, 2017, after widespread criticism of its terms and the process used to award it.

**Mississippi Youth Court Judge Resigns After Controversial Order Involving Mother and Baby**

Amid continuing debate over court fees, bail and the treatment of low-income defendants, the resignation of a youth court judge in Pearl, Mississippi, has drawn attention to a case involving a young mother and her infant.

Judge John Shirley, who served on the Pearl Youth Court, resigned after issuing an order in 2016 involving a woman identified in court documents as “Mother A.” According to reporting by *The Clarion-Ledger* and legal advocates who reviewed the case, the order prevented the woman from seeing her baby while she addressed unpaid court fees. The restriction reportedly remained in place for more than a year.

The case began when Mother A and a friend were stopped by police while driving through Pearl. Both women reportedly had misdemeanor warrants related to minor offenses. Mother A had her baby with her, and a relative came to the scene to take custody of the child.

The matter was then brought before the Pearl Youth Court. Court records cited in reports said Shirley placed the infant with the grandmother and issued a no-contact order barring the mother from seeing the baby until the outstanding fees were paid. The order also reportedly limited the mother’s contact with her grandmother while the child was present.

The circumstances of the order prompted criticism from civil rights attorneys, who questioned whether a parent’s ability to pay court costs should determine access to a child. Cliff Johnson, director of the Roderick and Solange MacArthur Justice Center at the University of Mississippi School of Law, called the reported order deeply troubling and said such cases raise serious concerns about the use of monetary conditions in youth court proceedings.

The case has also renewed broader questions about how courts handle unpaid fees and misdemeanor warrants, particularly when defendants lack the resources to pay. Legal advocates have argued that financial penalties can create additional barriers for people already struggling to navigate the justice system.

Shirley’s resignation was reported after the case came to public attention. Public reports did not establish that the resignation was solely connected to the order, and the judge’s departure did not by itself resolve the questions raised about the proceedings.

The case remains an example cited by critics of court practices that can place low-income families at risk of prolonged separation. It also illustrates how decisions made during routine encounters with law enforcement and lower courts can have significant consequences for parents and children.

**Washington Man Charged in Father’s Killing Had Ties to Far-Right Online Communities**

Washington State is often associated with progressive politics, but the region is also home to a range of extremist and far-right groups. Researchers and journalists have documented white-nationalist activity in the Pacific Northwest, including in rural communities north of Seattle.

That broader political landscape became part of the public discussion after a 2017 killing on Samish Island in Skagit County. Lane Davis, then 33, was accused of killing his father, Charles Davis, at the family’s home. The case drew additional attention because Lane Davis had previously been active in far-right online communities.

Davis was known online as “Seattle4Truth,” a name he used on platforms including Reddit and YouTube. He also contributed to The Ralph Retort, a website associated with the so-called alt-right, and had worked for commentator Milo Yiannopoulos, according to reporting at the time.

Authorities said the killing followed a dispute at the home. Court documents and contemporaneous news reports described an argument in which Davis’s father referred to him as a Nazi and sought to have him leave the house. Davis’s mother called 911 after the attack. The case was investigated as a homicide, and Davis was charged in connection with his father’s death.

The circumstances drew attention partly because Davis was not widely known in the area as a violent person. Neighbors and acquaintances described him as someone they had seen around town, while his online activity presented a more aggressive political identity. His public posts and associations placed him within a network of internet personalities and activists who promoted racist, antisemitic, or otherwise extremist views.

That distinction is important. Political extremism and violent crime are not interchangeable, and online affiliation alone does not establish why a person committed a particular act. In Davis’s case, investigators and prosecutors had to address the specific evidence surrounding the dispute, the killing, and his mental state rather than simply his internet persona.

The case also affected people who knew the family or lived nearby. Samish Island is a rural community connected to the mainland by a road through farmland. Residents and visitors commonly associate the area with homes, farms, wildlife, and community gatherings rather than with national political controversies. The alleged killing brought an intensely local event into the national conversation about the alt-right and political radicalization.

Davis’s online history had already attracted attention before the killing. He participated in internet forums and produced commentary that reflected far-right views, and his connections to prominent figures in that movement made the case more widely reported than a typical local homicide. Those links, however, were part of the background to the case, not proof that an entire political movement or region was responsible for the crime.

The incident occurred during a period when the alt-right was receiving increased public attention. Online communities that had once operated largely on the margins were becoming more visible through rallies, social media campaigns, and political commentary. Critics argued that the movement’s rhetoric helped normalize racism and harassment, while supporters described it as an alternative political current. Researchers and law-enforcement agencies continued to distinguish between protected political speech, extremist organizing, and criminal conduct.

The killing of Charles Davis remains a tragic example of how a family dispute can intersect with a person’s public ideological identity. It also illustrates the limits of drawing broad conclusions from a single case. Davis’s political views and online associations were relevant to understanding his background, but they do not by themselves explain the violence or establish a direct connection between national political figures and the homicide.

What is known is that a Washington man with a documented history of far-right online activity was accused of killing his father during a conflict at their home. The criminal case centered on that alleged act, the evidence collected by investigators, and the legal questions raised by the prosecution and defense. Any wider claims about political movements, local communities, or the causes of extremism require evidence beyond the case itself.

According to a statement attributed to principal Waylon Bates, failure to comply could result in reduced playing time or limits on participation, at the discretion of the head coach and principal. Continued noncompliance could lead to removal from the team.

The policy said Parkway was seeking to maintain a positive environment for sporting events and avoid disruptions to athletic contests. It did not specify how the rule would be applied in every circumstance, and public reporting at the time did not establish whether any students had been disciplined under it.

Trump called on team owners to discipline or dismiss players who did not stand, but his comments were not a federal order requiring schools or sports organizations to adopt similar policies.

Critics argued that a rule governing how students must behave during the anthem could itself raise questions about political expression and free speech. Some opponents also said that punishing athletes for a protest could cause additional students to participate in demonstrations.

The Louisiana High School Athletic Association has allowed schools to establish certain local policies governing their athletic programs, but that does not necessarily resolve whether a particular rule is constitutional. The authority of public schools to regulate student conduct can depend on the wording of the policy, the setting, the type of expression involved and the consequences imposed.

The debate also drew attention to a 1943 Supreme Court decision, *West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette*. In that case, the court ruled that public schools could not compel students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance when doing so conflicted with their beliefs. The decision overturned an earlier ruling that had permitted such requirements.

The plaintiffs in *Barnette* were Jehovah’s Witnesses, whose religious beliefs prevented them from saluting national symbols. The Supreme Court’s majority opinion, however, framed the case more broadly as one involving freedom of speech and belief.

Justice Robert Jackson, writing for the majority, stated that constitutional protections for speech, press, assembly and worship could not be restricted on insufficient grounds. He also wrote that public authorities could not compel individuals to “utter what is not in his mind.”

The decision is commonly cited in disputes over compelled speech, but its application to athletic participation is not automatic. Courts have recognized that schools may impose rules related to safety, order and team activities, while also limiting the government’s ability to punish students for protected expression. Whether sitting or kneeling during the anthem is protected in a specific school setting would depend on the facts and applicable law.

Some legal observers have noted that extracurricular activities are still connected to public schools and are not automatically exempt from constitutional requirements. At the same time, schools may argue that participation on an athletic team involves additional eligibility standards that do not apply in ordinary classroom settings.

The Parkway policy therefore prompted questions about the balance between team rules and students’ rights rather than establishing a clear nationwide legal precedent. The school’s action was one local response to a broader controversy over the national anthem, patriotism and racial inequality.

Trump’s remarks about NFL protests intensified that controversy in 2017, while players and their supporters said the demonstrations were intended to call attention to racial injustice and police treatment of Black Americans. The debate subsequently spread beyond professional sports to colleges, high schools and other public institutions.

Whether a student may be required to stand during the anthem, and whether a school may penalize a student for refusing, can vary according to state law, school policy and constitutional interpretation. The Parkway announcement highlighted those unresolved questions but did not, by itself, show that high schools nationwide had adopted similar rules or that the policy had been upheld by a court.

Medicaid Directors Raise Concerns About GOP Health Bill

On Thursday, the National Association of Medicaid Directors sent Congress a letter expressing concerns about the proposed overhaul of Medicaid in the Graham-Cassidy health bill. The association represents state Medicaid agencies, but the letter should not be characterized as a formal statement by every Medicaid director in the country.

In its letter, NAMD warned that the bill would make major changes to Medicaid financing. The proposal included per-capita limits on federal Medicaid funding and an option for states to use block grants. Under those arrangements, federal support would be determined through fixed formulas rather than rising automatically with enrollment or medical costs.

The association said the changes could shift significant financial responsibility from the federal government to the states. It also warned that states with growing Medicaid enrollment or higher health-care costs could face difficult budget decisions if federal funding did not keep pace.

“The scope of this work, and the resources required to support state planning and implementation activities, cannot be overstated,” the letter said. States, it added, would need to develop strategies, make infrastructure and systems changes, adjust provider and managed-care contracts, and undertake other administrative work.

NAMD also questioned whether states could complete those tasks within the proposed two-year implementation period. The organization said many states would have difficulty doing so, particularly if the legislation did not provide sufficient federal support for the planning and technical changes involved.

“With only a few legislative days left for the entire process to conclude,” the letter said, “there clearly is not sufficient time for policymakers, Governors, Medicaid Directors, or other critical stakeholders to engage in the thoughtful deliberation necessary to ensure successful long-term reforms.”

The letter came as Senate Republicans worked to advance the bill through the budget-reconciliation process. That procedure can allow certain legislation to pass the Senate with a simple majority, rather than the 60 votes generally needed to overcome a filibuster. The timetable was tied to the end of the 2017 fiscal year, creating pressure to act before September 30.

At the time, the Congressional Budget Office had not completed a full analysis of Graham-Cassidy. That absence drew criticism from opponents, who argued that lawmakers and the public should have access to an independent estimate of the bill’s effects before a vote.

The proposal faced opposition from health-care organizations, state officials and some Republican senators. Critics said its changes to Medicaid and the individual insurance market could increase uncertainty for states and for people who relied on coverage under the Affordable Care Act.

NAMD’s letter did not by itself determine the bill’s prospects in Congress, but it underscored the administrative and financial concerns state Medicaid agencies said they would face if the proposal became law.

**Jack Link’s Beef Jerky Ad Draws Criticism Over References to Genetics and Norse Mythology (VIDEO)**

Jack Link’s, a popular maker of beef jerky, released an advertisement featuring Green Bay Packers linebacker Clay Matthews that has prompted criticism online. The 30-second spot promotes the idea that protein and exercise can contribute to building muscle, using exaggerated humor and fantasy-style imagery.

At the beginning of the ad, Matthews says: “I’m the product of hard work, superior genetics, Norse mythology, and protein.” The commercial then shows animated primates repairing muscle fibers, followed by footage of Matthews displaying his physique.

Some viewers have argued that the references to “superior genetics” and “Norse mythology” carry associations with white supremacist ideology. Certain extremist groups have used racial theories, Nazi symbolism and distorted versions of Norse religious traditions in their propaganda. However, those associations do not by themselves establish that the commercial is intended to promote Nazism, antisemitism or white supremacy.

In the advertisement, the phrase “superior genetics” appears alongside references to hard work and protein as part of a humorous explanation for Matthews’ athletic build. The commercial does not identify a race, endorse racial hierarchy or make a political statement.

The mention of Norse mythology has also been interpreted by some critics through the lens of extremist groups that have adopted Norse symbols and religious themes. Those groups represent a particular political use of the tradition, while Norse mythology itself is a broad body of stories and beliefs that predates modern racial ideologies.

The ad’s use of primates has similarly been criticized because racist propaganda has historically used animal imagery to demean racial and religious minorities. In the commercial, however, the animals are presented as part of a cartoon-like explanation of muscle recovery. There is no clear indication in the spot that the imagery is directed at Black people, Jewish people or any other group.

The controversy illustrates how advertising language and imagery can take on different meanings depending on the audience and the historical associations attached to particular terms. Words such as “genetics” and references to Norse mythology have appeared in extremist rhetoric, but they are also used in nonpolitical contexts, including sports, entertainment and marketing.

There is no evidence in the advertisement itself that Jack Link’s intended to appeal to Nazis or other white supremacists. The commercial appears to use exaggerated athletic imagery and a comedic tone to market beef jerky, rather than to advance a racial or religious ideology.

Viewers may still find the language or visual style insensitive, particularly given the history of racial pseudoscience and extremist appropriation of Norse symbols. But interpreting the commercial as an explicit declaration of white supremacy goes beyond what the advertisement shows.

Trump Judicial Nominee Faced Criticism Over Remarks About Transgender Students and Conversion Therapy

Donald Trump’s nominee for a federal judgeship in Texas faced criticism from LGBT rights organizations over past remarks concerning transgender students, same-sex marriage and so-called conversion therapy.

Afterward, Trump said on Twitter that the leaders he met had agreed with much or all of his remarks.

“A great and important day at the United Nations. Met with leaders of many nations who agree with much (or all) of what I stated in my speech!” Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) September 20, 2017

There is no public evidence showing that the world leaders attending the meetings unanimously supported Trump’s positions. Diplomatic meetings and applause at the General Assembly do not provide a reliable measure of international approval, and reactions to his speech varied.

The Pew survey, conducted earlier this year, found that confidence in Trump was substantially lower in many countries than confidence in President Barack Obama during the final years of Obama’s presidency. The survey measured whether respondents had confidence in the U.S. president to do the right thing regarding world affairs; it did not determine whether governments agreed with every part of Trump’s speech.

Confidence was particularly low in several U.S. allied countries. In South Korea, for example, 17 percent of respondents said they had confidence in Trump, compared with 88 percent who expressed confidence in Obama in a comparable 2015 survey. Mexico also recorded a sharp decline in confidence after Trump took office.

The survey did not show that only two nations viewed Trump favorably. Rather, it found that opinions differed by country and by question. Some respondents in Israel and Russia expressed relatively high confidence in Trump, while other countries surveyed reported much lower levels. Favorability toward the United States also did not always move in tandem with views of the president.

Public opposition to several of Trump’s major policies was also evident in international polling. The Pew findings showed broad disagreement with some elements of his approach to climate change, trade and immigration, although the level of support or opposition varied from country to country. Such surveys measure public opinion, not the official positions of governments represented at the United Nations.

Republicans who controlled the Senate supported the increase, while critics argued that Congress should more closely examine the military’s requirements and the effect of additional defense spending on the federal deficit. Because the NDAA was an authorization measure, however, its passage did not by itself make the spending available or constitute a violation of the budget law. Congress could—and later did—change the spending limits through subsequent legislation.

The debate also renewed questions about the size and priorities of the U.S. defense budget. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the United States accounted for about 36 percent of global military spending in 2016, more than any other country. U.S. military spending was several times higher than China’s and substantially higher than Russia’s, although estimates vary depending on how countries’ defense expenditures are measured.

Some lawmakers and advocacy groups argued that a portion of the proposed increase could instead be directed toward domestic priorities, including higher education, health care, infrastructure, or deficit reduction. A survey conducted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch of more than 300 companies reportedly asked executives how they would use money brought back from overseas. The leading responses included paying down debt and buying back company shares.

Stock buybacks have become a central point of criticism surrounding repatriation holidays. When a company buys its own shares, the reduced number of shares outstanding can increase earnings per share and may support the stock price. Buybacks can benefit shareholders and executives whose compensation is tied to share performance, although they do not necessarily lead to new factories, stores or jobs.

The United States adopted a similar repatriation tax holiday in 2004, allowing companies to bring certain foreign earnings home at a substantially reduced tax rate. Subsequent analyses found that much of the money was returned to shareholders through buybacks and dividends rather than being used for increased domestic investment. The policy’s effect on hiring and broader economic growth has remained disputed.

Some companies that repatriated money during that period also reduced their workforces, but that does not establish that the tax holiday caused those layoffs. Corporate decisions about employment and investment are influenced by many factors, including demand, technology and industry conditions.

The same questions apply to any future tax break for repatriated profits. Companies could use the money to invest, pay down debt, increase dividends, repurchase shares or hold cash. The policy’s overall economic impact would depend on how businesses used the funds and whether the resulting activity generated additional demand.

Critics argue that policies focused on corporate tax reductions may provide greater immediate benefits to shareholders than to workers, while supporters say lower taxes can improve incentives for investment. The debate over repatriation therefore centers on whether companies would use the savings to expand their operations or primarily strengthen their balance sheets and return money to investors.

After a terrorist attack in London, President Donald Trump used a social-media post to claim that his administration had made more progress against ISIS than the Obama administration.

By the time Trump took office, ISIS had lost much of the territory it controlled in Iraq, although it still held important areas in Syria and the Iraqi city of Mosul. At the same time, civilian-casualty monitors reported deaths from coalition operations in Iraq and Syria, though determining responsibility for individual casualties can be difficult. The administration disputed some estimates and said it took steps to avoid civilian harm.

ISIS propaganda has used U.S. military operations and civilian deaths in its messaging, as terrorist groups have done throughout the conflict. But claims that any one administration’s policies directly caused changes in recruitment are difficult to substantiate.

In military terms, Trump inherited an ongoing campaign in which ISIS had already lost most of its territorial control but continued to operate as an insurgent and terrorist organization. His administration continued and intensified that campaign, while relying on plans and partnerships developed during the Obama years.

Trump could reasonably point to battlefield gains during his first nine months, including the capture of Mosul. But the broader reduction of ISIS’s territory and military strength had begun well before he took office.

The record therefore does not support a simple conclusion that either president alone defeated ISIS. The campaign was conducted over multiple years by U.S. and allied forces under both administrations, and the group remained a threat despite its territorial losses.

**Soviet Officer Stanislav Petrov, Known for Rejecting False Nuclear Alert, Dies at 77**

Stanislav Petrov, a former Soviet lieutenant colonel who became known for his role in a 1983 false nuclear warning, died on May 19, 2017, at his home in Fryazino, northeast of Moscow. His death was reported publicly several months later. He was 77.

Petrov’s story gained international attention through the 2014 documentary *The Man Who Saved the World*. The film examined how his decision during one of the most tense periods of the Cold War helped prevent a false warning from escalating into a possible confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union.

The incident took place on September 26, 1983, when Petrov was serving as the duty officer at the Serpukhov-15 early-warning facility near Moscow. The Soviet warning system reported that a missile had been launched from the United States. A short time later, it indicated that four more missiles had followed.

Petrov was responsible for assessing the warning and reporting it up the chain of command. Instead of treating the alert as a confirmed attack, he judged that it was probably a system malfunction. His reasoning included the small number of missiles detected and the lack of confirmation from other Soviet monitoring systems, including ground-based radar.

The alert was later determined to have been caused by sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds and being misinterpreted by Soviet satellites. Petrov’s decision did not by itself control whether the Soviet Union would launch nuclear weapons, but it helped prevent a false warning from immediately being treated as an actual attack.

The episode occurred during a particularly tense period in U.S.-Soviet relations. Earlier that month, the Soviet Union had shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, and military and political tensions between the two nuclear powers were high. The false alert remained classified for years, and Petrov did not become widely known outside the Soviet military until accounts of the incident emerged in the 1990s.

Petrov later received international recognition for his actions. In 2006, the Association of World Citizens presented him with an award at the United Nations in New York honoring his role in preventing a possible nuclear catastrophe. He also received the German Media Prize in 2012 and the Dresden Peace Prize in 2013.

Petrov generally rejected descriptions of himself as a hero, saying that he had been carrying out his duty and making a professional judgment based on the information available to him. His story has since been cited as an example of the dangers of relying on automated warning systems during periods of international tension.

“Few, if any, Administrations have done more in just 7 months than the Trump A. Bills passed, regulations killed, border, military, ISIS, SC!” he wrote, referring to the Supreme Court vacancy filled during his first year.

The two messages reflected a recurring pattern in Trump’s public statements: he claimed credit for administrative actions and congressional achievements while also blaming Democrats for blocking his legislative agenda. The situation was more complicated than either description suggested. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress, but the Senate’s filibuster rules meant that many major bills required Democratic support.

Trump had made similar complaints earlier in the year. In February, he blamed Democrats for delays in confirming Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price while saying that efforts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act were advancing. In March, he criticized Democrats for not approving his full Cabinet.

By July, Trump was also accusing Senate Democrats of slowing the confirmation of presidential nominees. “They can't win so all they do is slow things down & obstruct!” he wrote.

Other posts portrayed Democrats as a party of obstruction and argued that their use of the courts and procedural delays was making it more difficult to address national security issues.

At the same time, Trump regularly described his administration’s performance in sweeping terms, emphasizing executive actions, regulatory changes, military policy and the confirmation of a Supreme Court justice. Those claims did not change the basic limits imposed by the Senate’s rules or the need for Congress to approve legislation.

The result was a familiar contradiction. Trump wanted to present himself as a highly productive president while arguing that congressional rules and Democratic opposition prevented him from accomplishing more. His August tweets captured both arguments, even though the two positions sat uneasily together.

REPORT: Mueller Expands Team to Investigate Russian Election Interference

Special Counsel Robert Mueller has assembled a sizable team of attorneys to investigate Russia’s interference in the 2016 presidential election, including possible contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian officials.

According to a report by The Daily Beast, Mueller’s team includes 16 attorneys with extensive experience in federal law enforcement and other areas of litigation. The investigators are working in secure facilities in Washington, including a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF, where classified information can be handled.

The Daily Beast described the group as a “miniature Justice Department” and published background information on members of the team. Most of the attorneys have worked as federal prosecutors, while others bring private-sector or specialized legal experience to the investigation.

Mueller’s office has broad authority to examine potential coordination between the campaign and the Russian government, as well as other matters that may arise during the inquiry. Investigators can issue subpoenas and question witnesses under oath when authorized to do so. Knowingly making false statements to federal investigators can also carry criminal penalties, whether or not a person is testifying before a grand jury.

Mueller has also convened a federal grand jury in connection with the investigation. The use of a grand jury allows prosecutors to obtain documents and testimony, but it does not by itself indicate that criminal charges will be filed.

The investigation remained ongoing, and the appointment of additional attorneys and the use of investigative tools did not establish wrongdoing by President Donald Trump, his campaign, or members of his administration.

House Democrat Proposes Bar on Federal Spending at Trump Properties

Lawmakers were preparing to consider a broad spending measure covering much of the federal government, with a deadline for funding approaching. Failure to approve the legislation or another temporary measure could have led to a government shutdown. The bill was expected to face debate over amendments, including one proposed by a Tennessee Democrat targeting federal spending at properties connected to President Donald Trump.

Representative Steve Cohen said he planned to offer amendments that would prohibit federal agencies from using appropriated funds at businesses owned, operated or financially connected to the president. The proposal would apply to properties identified in Trump’s financial-disclosure documents, including hotels, country clubs and resorts.

If adopted, the measure could affect federal agencies that pay for lodging, meetings, security arrangements or other services at Trump-branded properties. Events involving government officials that were held at those locations could instead be moved elsewhere, unless the costs were covered without federal funds.

Cohen has argued that federal spending at the president’s businesses creates an appearance of a conflict of interest. His proposal comes amid broader scrutiny of Trump’s decision to retain ownership of his businesses while serving as president rather than placing them in a blind trust or fully divesting.

In a statement, Cohen said:

“Congress should not allow the President to use his office to profit himself and his family. The President’s refusal to divest from his privately owned businesses creates a conflict of interest when steering federal spending to his resorts and other businesses. The American people should have total confidence that the President is serving their interest, not his own financial enrichment.”

Cohen also criticized Trump over concerns involving profits connected to foreign governments and said Congress should examine whether those arrangements comply with constitutional requirements. Those issues were the subject of ongoing legal and political debate.

The amendments would need support from the Republican-controlled Congress to pass. Even if they received a vote, their prospects were uncertain, as Republican leaders generally controlled the appropriations process and could decline to bring particular amendments before the full House.

The proposed restrictions reflect a larger debate over how federal agencies should handle transactions involving businesses owned by a sitting president. Supporters said the policy could reduce potential conflicts and reassure the public that government spending was based on practical considerations rather than personal financial interests. Opponents could argue that existing procurement and ethics rules already govern such spending and that a blanket prohibition could complicate agency operations.

Cohen’s proposal was therefore unlikely to change the spending bill on its own, but it could bring additional attention to the question of whether federal money should be spent at properties tied to the president.

**Laura Ingraham Website Criticized Over Photo Used to Illustrate Trump Rally Crowd**

A website associated with conservative commentator Laura Ingraham faced criticism after readers questioned a photograph used in coverage of a Donald Trump rally.

The image was presented as showing a large crowd of Trump supporters. Online users, however, identified it as a photograph from the 2016 Cleveland Cavaliers championship parade rather than from the rally described in the accompanying report. The photograph therefore did not provide reliable evidence of the size of the Trump event.

Images from large public gatherings are sometimes reused in political commentary, making the original source and date important when assessing claims about crowd sizes. In this case, comparisons between the image and the venue shown in the report prompted questions about whether the photograph accurately represented the event.

The episode also renewed discussion of earlier criticism directed at Ingraham. In 2016, a photograph circulated online appearing to show her raising her arm toward an image of Trump during an appearance at the Conservative Political Action Conference. Some viewers interpreted the gesture as resembling a Nazi salute. The image’s meaning was disputed, and it does not by itself establish that Ingraham intended to make such a gesture.

Similar misinformation has circulated among political groups on both sides. In one example, the Virginia Republican Party shared an article claiming that Rosa Parks’ daughter had praised Trump as a “civil rights hero.” The claim was false: Parks did not have children. The article was nevertheless reposted by users on social media before the error was noted.

The incidents highlight the importance of checking photographs, captions and original sources before sharing political material. Crowd-size claims and viral political images can spread quickly, particularly when they reinforce existing views about a candidate or party.

The disputed photograph was used as a featured image in the online article.
